raw: 14.1 Supply Chain Operations as Strategic Intelligence Tradecraft
teaching_note: A supply-chain assessment follows trust and artifact dependencies across development, build, distribution and use; it does not teach acquisition operations. Package identity, vulnerability affectedness, deployment and exploitability are separate claims. Analytic standards support distinguishing observations from judgments, not presuming compromise from a supplier relationship [@ageint297].
title: Supply Chain Operations as Strategic Intelligence Tradecraft

teaching_note: The inherited 'six-month' phrase is a narrative framing, not a verified duration for every phase or victim. Separate development, distribution, installation, follow-on activity and discovery windows; receiving an affected update does not by itself establish that follow-on intrusion occurred. The vendor glossary is secondary orientation rather than primary evidence for exact timing, operator identity or the efficacy of its suggested controls, so those particulars remain bounded or unknown.
title: SolarWinds/SUNBURST: The Six-Month Patient Operation

raw: 14.3 XZ Utils/Jia Tan: Two-Year Social Engineering and Trust Infiltration[^74][^75][^76]
teaching_note: Separate a public contributor handle, observed repository actions and an inferred human or organizational identity; the handle is not proof of a person's legal identity or sponsor. The inherited 'two-year' narrative does not establish the duration of every preparatory act or the causal effect of each social interaction. These secondary accounts motivate artifact and trust-boundary analysis, not a reconstruction of covert recruitment or an attribution conclusion.
title: XZ Utils/Jia Tan: Two-Year Social Engineering and Trust Infiltration

raw: 14.3.1 Sock Puppetry as HUMINT Cover Tradecraft[^76]
teaching_note: Sock-puppetry allegations concern possible common control of multiple accounts; matching tone or pressure on a maintainer does not establish that control. The analogy to HUMINT cover is an interpretive comparison, not proof that a formal human-intelligence operation occurred. Preserve distinct account records and unsupported linkage hypotheses, and do not provide impersonation, engagement or account-creation procedures.
title: Sock Puppetry as HUMINT Cover Tradecraft

teaching_note: A CVSS score expresses severity under a specified scoring version and vector, not a 100% compromise probability or proof that every installation is exploitable. Treat the inherited 10.0 label as a reported rating requiring a dated advisory, vector and affected configuration before reuse. Distinguish the exact source/release artifact, build conditions, installed binary and reachable vulnerable behaviour; no mechanism reproduction or exploit execution is required.
title: CVE-2024-3094: CVSS 10.0 Backdoor Mechanism

teaching_note: The raw inherited APT29/SVR wording is an attribution hypothesis, not an established conclusion supported by this encyclopedia citation. Patience, social engineering and software tampering are non-exclusive similarities that cannot identify an operator or sponsor. Record the comparison as unsupported and retain alternative actors or unknown control; do not turn stylistic resemblance into a nationality claim.
title: Attribution Limits: The Inherited APT29/SVR Similarity Hypothesis

raw: 14.3.4 "Friendly Yet Aggressive and Persistent" Social Engineering Signature[^76]
teaching_note: The inherited phrase 'friendly yet aggressive and persistent' is a description, not a validated behavioural signature, diagnostic test or evidence of malicious intent. It can also describe ordinary disagreement, urgency or volunteer-project stress; judging people from it would generate unquantified false positives. Analyse supplied process facts such as review concentration and unexplained artifact changes instead of profiling maintainers or contributors.
title: Interaction Style Is Not an Attribution Signature

raw: 14.4 Open-Source Maintainer Targeting as an Acquisition Operation[^76]
teaching_note: The acquisition-operation analogy must not replace evidence about permissions, review and artifact changes. A maintainer's workload or a contributor's persistence does not establish targeting, collusion or culpability. The safe lesson is a non-personal review of how a supplied project's trust decisions were recorded, not collection about real maintainers or instructions for gaining their trust.
title: Open-Source Maintainer Targeting as an Acquisition Operation

teaching_note: Keep SBOM inventory, build provenance, signing identity and source review separate: a declared inventory is not completeness proof, and a valid signature does not prove benign contents; SSDF is process guidance rather than case-specific efficacy evidence [@ageint304]. In a completed fictional packet, M1 declares 'atlas-parser' 2.4/digest D1, advisory A1 concerns supplier Q's 2.4/D2, and the installed digest is absent, yielding 'name/version match only; deployment, affectedness and exploitability unknown'. Classroom trust card T1 expects builder B1, signer S1 and source revision R1: supplied release P1 has artifact D1 but provenance subject D2, so subject binding fails, while P2 has matching subject D1 and a valid S1 signature but builder B2, so it fails the separate expected-builder check; neither is accepted under T1. A supplied component list omitting dependency status is incomplete evidence, not evidence of no dependencies, and a third packet passing T1 would establish only those checks, not code safety. Same-name supplier R is a negative control against name-only joins; stop at missing identity/deployment evidence and retain each failed expectation, following the distinct digest, signature and expectation checks in the chosen SLSA v1.1 guidance [@official_slsa_supply_chain_security_specification], without executing any artifact.
title: Countermeasures: SBOM, SLSA Framework, Sigstore

raw: 14.6 Threat Intelligence Sharing for ICS Supply Chain (arXiv Survey)[^77]
teaching_note: The inspected arXiv v3 study (27 January 2026) examines three incidents, 196 procedure examples across 79 techniques and 22 malware families, plus nine vulnerability advisories, with LLM-assisted observable extraction [@ageint077]. Its representation and technical-detail findings are bounded by that corpus and extraction method, not proof that all ICS sharing is ineffective; proposed STIX extensions are not validated prevention outcomes. In a fictional report, 'component Z changed' can be represented as text but lacks version, time and observation method, so the worked result is 'representable assertion; insufficient context for a justified component-change judgment'. Adding a second serialized copy supplies no missing context, while a supplied correction to 'documentation changed' withdraws the software-change interpretation. No live ICS interaction, detector deployment or empirical efficacy claim follows from this record exercise.
title: Threat Intelligence Sharing for ICS Supply Chain (arXiv Survey)
